newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Toyota says US export cut not political.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Toyota says US export cut not political.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp's plans to trim its car exports to the United States this year reflect an expected dip in demand, not worries about U.S.-Japan trade friction, a top official at the carmaker said on Friday.

Dismissing Japanese media reports that the two percent reduction was made for political reasons, Toyota executive vice president Akira Yokoi told Reuters that the company expected total U.S. car demand to slip below 15 million vehicles in the current business year from 15.32 million the year before.
Toyota, Japan's largest carmaker, plans to export 480,000 cars to North America in fiscal year 1997/98, which began on April 1, down 10,000 units from 1996/97.
"We did not lower the projection with (political) intentions," said Yokoi, who is in charge of Toyota's overseas operations, in an interview.

"Early this year, we expected the U.S. market to remain flat this year against the previous year, but now we see signs indicating the possibility that it will fall short of 15 million units," Yokoi said.
"But exports (in 1997/98) at last year's levels can be expected if (the U.S. market) does not fall below 15 million," he added.
Despite the lower exports, Toyota plans to boost local output in North America to 850,000 units in 1997/98 from 800,000 units the year before, a company spokesman said earlier this week.
Yokoi estimated Toyota's total U.S. sales at 1.2 million units in 1997/98, little changed from 1.18 million units in the prior year.

He added that, in Europe, Toyota wants to raise output over the next 10 years to more than 65 percent of the vehicles it sells there, although he declined to specify in which country the automaker is likely to build a new production plant.
Toyota last year built 117,000 cars at its only European plant in central England. The company has said it plans to boost European sales to 600,000 cars by 2000 from 420,000 in 1996.
Yokoi said he expected vehicle demand in Europe would remain flat this business year.
The yen's recent weakness has boosted Japan's car exports by making Japanese goods cheaper in dollar terms.
This has particularly fuelled worries that Japan and the United States may be heading towards yet another bitter trade dispute.

Japan's latest trade figures stunned market watchers, revealing that the overall trade surplus surged 163.7 percent in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen while the surplus with the United States jumped 174.1 percent to 468.97 billion yen.
Economists attributed the increase primarily to car exports.
